title: The Bakery Before the Bookshop
scene: Two friends planned to visit a bookshop before buying pastries. The bakery closes earlier, so Mia suggests reversing the order and explains why. They check the bookshop's hours and enjoy both places without rushing.
sceneJa: 友人と本屋を見てからパン屋に寄るつもりだったが、パン屋のほうが早く閉まる。ミアが順番を入れ替える提案をし、理由を伝える。営業時間を確認して、慌てずに両方を楽しむ。

chunks.en: We had planned to browse the bookshop
chunks.ja: 本屋を見て回る予定だった

chunks.en: but the bakery closed at four.
chunks.ja: でもパン屋は4時に閉まる

chunks.en: 'What if we go to the bakery first
chunks.ja: 「先にパン屋に行くのはどう？

chunks.en: and leave the books for later?'
just to get there before closing,' she said.
chunks.ja: 閉店前に着こうと急ぐ必要もないよ」と彼女は言った
僕は「なるほど、確かにね」と答えた

chunks.en: We can always take our time
chunks.ja: ゆっくり時間をかけられるし
本屋の営業時間を確認した
本屋は6時まで開いていたので
本を眺めながら歩いた
時計を気にすることなく

questions.question: Which split keeps Mia's suggestion as a natural speaking unit?
options: What if / we go to the bakery / first and leave the books for later?
What if we go to the bakery first / and leave the books for later?
What / if we go to the bakery first and / leave the books for later?
questions.explanation: 'What if we go to the bakery first?' gently proposes a change. The second unit adds what to do later.

questions.question: What does 'We can always take our time at the bookshop afterward' mean?
options: They must spend exactly one hour in the bookshop.
They have the option of browsing without rushing later.
They have to skip the bookshop entirely.
questions.explanation: 'Can always' suggests an available option; 'take our time' means not hurry. It does not mean they always visit bookshops.

questions.question: Why does Mia suggest going to the bakery first?
options: She has lost interest in books.
The bakery closes earlier, and changing the order avoids a rush.
She wants to avoid buying pastries.
questions.explanation: Mia proposes a new order and gives a practical reason: the bakery closes earlier, while the bookshop stays open longer.

speak: Imagine: you and a friend want to visit two places, but one closes sooner. Read: picture the bakery sign and bookshop shelves. Chunk: keep 'What if we ... first?', 'That way, ...', and 'We can always ...' together. Understand: 'What if we ...?' gently proposes a plan; 'That way' introduces the benefit; 'can always' offers a possible solution. Check: answer three questions. Speak (30 seconds): suggest switching the order of two errands. Say 'What if we ... first?', explain 'That way, ...', and offer a fallback with 'We can always ...'. Final Read: read all six sentences without Japanese, sounding practical rather than bossy; pause naturally after 'That way'.
review: New: 'What if we ... first?' (先に〜するのはどう？), 'That way, ...' (そうすれば〜), 'We can always ...' (〜する手もある／いつでも〜できる). Reuse Lesson 101 'Fair enough' (なるほど、確かに) to accept a plan rather than a borrowing boundary; Lesson 92/101 'Just to make sure' (念のため) to check opening hours rather than a meeting entrance or handover. Compared with the previous 14 lessons (90–103), this focuses on sequencing errands and explaining the benefit, not declining an invitation, requesting permission, or fixing a misunderstanding. Usage: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/what-if and https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/can-always .
